extraction.name: Geometry3K
extraction.description: Geometry3K is a large-scale benchmark for geometry problem solving, consisting of 3,002 multi-choice geometry problems collected from two high-school textbooks (grades 6-12). Each problem includes problem text in natural language, a geometry diagram, four candidate choices, and the correct answer. Unlike existing datasets, each problem is densely annotated with unified structural descriptions in formal language, covering diverse geometric shapes (lines, triangles, regular quadrilaterals, irregular quadrilaterals, circles, and other polygons) and problem goals. The dataset is divided into train (2,101), validation (300), and test (601) sets.
extraction.creator: Pan Lu, Ran Gong, Shibiao Jiang, Liang Qiu, Siyuan Huang, Xiaodan Liang, Song-Chun Zhu
extraction.publisher: UCLA, Zhejiang University, Sun Yat-sen University, Beijing Institute of General Artificial Intelligence, Peking University, Tsinghua University
extraction.citeAs: Lu, P., Gong, R., Jiang, S., Qiu, L., Huang, S., Liang, X., & Zhu, S.-C. (2021). Inter-GPS: Interpretable Geometry Problem Solving with Formal Language and Symbolic Reasoning. arXiv:2105.04165.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The data is collected from two popular textbooks for high school students across grades 6-12 by two online digital libraries (McGraw-Hill, Geometryonline). Groups of well-trained annotators with undergraduate degrees manually collect each problem with its problem text, geometry diagram, four candidate choices, and correct answer. Each problem is labeled with the corresponding problem goal and geometry shapes, and further annotated with dense formal language descriptions.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Two high-school geometry textbooks accessed via online digital libraries McGraw-Hill (https://www.mheducation.com/) and Geometryonline (www.geometryonline.com).
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Groups of well-trained annotators with undergraduate degrees manually collected each problem with its problem text, geometry diagram, four candidate choices, and correct answer. Each problem data is labeled with the corresponding problem goal and geometry shapes. Each problem text and diagram is further annotated with unified structural descriptions in formal language using 91 defined predicates across six categories (geometric shapes, unary geometric attributes, general geometric attributes, binary geometric relations, A-IsXOf-B-type geometric relations, and numerical attributes and relations).
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Amazon Mechanical Turk (used for human performance evaluation on the test split)
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human performance was evaluated on the test split via crowdsourcing. Each eligible annotator must have obtained a high school or higher degree and was asked to answer 10 problems in 25 minutes, with minimum 7 minutes on the problem set and 10 seconds per problem. Annotators not meeting requirements were filtered out. Humans achieved overall accuracy of 56.9%, while human experts (graduates majoring in science/engineering) achieved 90.9%.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotators for dataset construction: groups of well-trained annotators with undergraduate degrees. For human performance evaluation: AMT workers with at least high school degree; human experts were graduates majoring in science or engineering.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The work may inspire follow-up research in symbolic reasoning and interpretable models and facilitate education.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Less than 1% of problems in Geometry3K can be solved without the associated diagram, making it challenging. Current diagram parsing can fail with ambiguous annotations or multiple primitives; text parsing can struggle with nested expressions and uncertain references; the symbolic solver is not fully capable of solving complex problems with combined shapes and shaded areas.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing of geometry problem solving algorithms, including symbolic reasoning methods, neural geometry solvers, and problem parsers for both text and diagrams. Used to evaluate interpretable problem solving with formal language.
